prompt:
Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be a continuous function which is continuously differentiable on $(a,b)$. Show that for all $c\in[a,b]$ we have
$$|f(c)|\le \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx+\int_a^b|f'(x)|\,dx .$$
answer: Let $d$ be a minimum point of $|f|$ (or of $f$ after replacing $f$ by $-f$): $|f(d)|$ is at most the average of $|f|$, and $|f(c)|-|f(d)|\le\int_a^b|f'|$ by the fundamental theorem of calculus.

solutions.title: Compare with the minimum of $|f|$
solutions.body:
If $\int_a^b|f'|=\infty$ there is nothing to prove, so assume it is finite.

The function $|f|$ is continuous on the compact interval $[a,b]$, so it attains its minimum at some $d\in[a,b]$. Then
$$|f(d)|=\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b|f(d)|\,dx\le\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx .$$

Next, for $a<s<t<b$ the fundamental theorem of calculus gives $f(t)-f(s)=\int_s^t f'(x)\,dx$, hence $|f(t)-f(s)|\le\int_a^b|f'|$. Letting $s,t$ tend to the endpoints and using continuity of $f$ on $[a,b]$, this holds for all $s,t\in[a,b]$. In particular
$$|f(c)|-|f(d)|\le|f(c)-f(d)|\le\int_a^b|f'(x)|\,dx .$$

Adding the two inequalities gives
$$|f(c)|\le\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx+\int_a^b|f'(x)|\,dx. \quad\blacksquare$$

solutions.title: Average the pointwise estimate
solutions.body:
For every $x\in[a,b]$, as in the first solution, $|f(c)|\le|f(x)|+|f(c)-f(x)|\le|f(x)|+\int_a^b|f'|$. Integrating this inequality in $x$ over $[a,b]$ and dividing by $b-a$ gives exactly
$$|f(c)|\le\frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b|f(x)|\,dx+\int_a^b|f'(x)|\,dx. \quad\blacksquare$$

prompt:
Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n,\dots$ be real numbers. Show that the infinite series
$$\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{e^{i\lambda_n x}}{n^2}$$
converges uniformly over $\mathbb R$ to a continuous limit function $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$. Show, further, that the limit
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T}f(x)\,dx$$
exists.
answer: Uniform convergence by the Weierstrass M-test with $M_n=1/n^2$. Integrating term by term, $\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^Tf=\sum_n\frac1{n^2}\cdot\frac{\sin\lambda_nT}{\lambda_nT}$ (the factor is $1$ when $\lambda_n=0$), which tends to $\sum_{\lambda_n=0}1/n^2$.

solutions.title: M-test, then term-by-term limits
solutions.body:
**Uniform convergence and continuity.** Each term satisfies $\left|e^{i\lambda_nx}/n^2\right|=1/n^2$ and $\sum 1/n^2<\infty$, so by the Weierstrass M-test the series converges uniformly on $\mathbb R$. The partial sums are continuous, so the uniform limit $f$ is continuous.

**The mean value.** For real $\lambda$ and $T>0$ put
$$m_\lambda(T)=\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^Te^{i\lambda x}\,dx=\begin{cases}1,&\lambda=0,\\[2pt] \dfrac{\sin\lambda T}{\lambda T},&\lambda\neq 0,\end{cases}$$
(for $\lambda\neq0$ the imaginary part $\sin\lambda x$ is odd and integrates to $0$). Note $|m_\lambda(T)|\le1$ and, for $\lambda\neq 0$, $|m_\lambda(T)|\le\frac{1}{|\lambda|T}\to0$.

Because the series converges uniformly on $[-T,T]$, we may integrate term by term:
$$\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^Tf(x)\,dx=\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{m_{\lambda_n}(T)}{n^2}.$$

Let $L=\sum_{n:\lambda_n=0}\frac1{n^2}$. Given $\varepsilon>0$ choose $N$ with $\sum_{n>N}\frac1{n^2}<\varepsilon$. Then
$$\left|\sum_{n=1}^\infty\frac{m_{\lambda_n}(T)}{n^2}-L\right|\le\sum_{n\le N,\ \lambda_n\neq 0}\frac{1}{n^2|\lambda_n|T}+2\sum_{n>N}\frac1{n^2}<\frac{C_N}{T}+2\varepsilon,$$
where $C_N=\sum_{n\le N,\lambda_n\neq 0}\frac1{n^2|\lambda_n|}$ is a finite constant. For $T>C_N/\varepsilon$ the difference is less than $3\varepsilon$.

Hence the limit exists and
$$\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac1{2T}\int_{-T}^Tf(x)\,dx=\sum_{n:\ \lambda_n=0}\frac1{n^2}$$
(in particular it is $0$ if no $\lambda_n$ vanishes). $\blacksquare$

prompt: Let $U$ be a connected and simply connected open subset of the complex plane, and let $f$ be a holomorphic function on $U$. Suppose $a$ is a point of $U$ such that the Taylor series of $f$ at $a$ converges on an open disc $D$ that intersects the complement of $U$. Does it follow that $f$ extends to a holomorphic function on $U\cup D$? Give a proof or a counterexample.
answer: No. Take $U=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$, $f=\operatorname{Log}z$ (principal branch), $a=-1+\tfrac i2$, $D=D(a,|a|)$: the Taylor series is a branch of $\log$ on $D$ continuous across the negative axis, while $\operatorname{Log}$ jumps by $2\pi i$ there.

solutions.title: A branch cut counterexample
solutions.body:
**No.** Let $U=\mathbb C\setminus(-\infty,0]$ (a star-shaped, hence connected and simply connected, open set) and let $f(z)=\operatorname{Log}z=\ln|z|+i\operatorname{Arg}z$ with $\operatorname{Arg}z\in(-\pi,\pi)$. Let $a=-1+\frac i2$, so $|a|=\frac{\sqrt5}2$, and $D=\{z:|z-a|<|a|\}$.

*The Taylor series converges on $D$.* The disc $D$ does not contain $0$ and is simply connected, so there is a holomorphic branch $S$ of $\log z$ on $D$; choose it with $S(a)=f(a)$. Since $S$ is holomorphic on the disc $D$ centred at $a$, its Taylor series at $a$ converges to $S$ on $D$; and since $S=f$ near $a$, this is the Taylor series of $f$ at $a$.

*$D$ meets the complement of $U$:* $|-1-a|=\frac12<|a|$, so $-1\in D\setminus U$.

*No holomorphic extension exists.* Suppose $F$ is holomorphic on $U\cup D$ with $F=f$ on $U$. Both $F|_D$ and $S$ are holomorphic on the connected set $D$ and agree with $f$ near $a$, so $F=S$ on $D$ by the identity theorem. Now consider points $-1\pm i\varepsilon$ ($\varepsilon>0$ small); they lie in $D\cap U$. As $\varepsilon\to0^+$:
- $f(-1+i\varepsilon)\to\ln1+i\pi=i\pi$ and $f(-1-i\varepsilon)\to-i\pi$;
- but $f=F=S$ at these points and $S$ is continuous at $-1\in D$, so both limits equal $S(-1)$.

This gives $i\pi=-i\pi$, a contradiction. So $f$ does not extend to $U\cup D$.

(The point is that $D\cap U$ is disconnected: the identity theorem only forces agreement with the Taylor series on the component of $D\cap U$ containing $a$.) $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Let the function $f$ be holomorphic in the strip $-1<\operatorname{Im}z<1$, real on the real axis, and of positive imaginary part in the strip $0<\operatorname{Im}z<1$.

(a) Prove that $f$ has negative imaginary part in the strip $-1<\operatorname{Im}z<0$.

(b) Prove $f'(x)\ge0$ for $x$ real.

(c) Prove $f'(x)>0$ for $x$ real.
answer: (a) Reflection: $f(\bar z)=\overline{f(z)}$. (b) $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{f(x+ih)-f(x)}{ih}$ is real and equals $\lim\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)}{h}\ge0$. (c) If $f'(c)=0$ then $f(z)=f(c)+a_m(z-c)^m+\dots$ with $m\ge2$, $a_m\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}$, and $\operatorname{Im}f$ takes both signs on a small upper half-circle around $c$.

solutions.title: Schwarz reflection and local behaviour
solutions.body:
Let $D=\{z:-1<\operatorname{Im}z<1\}$; note $D$ is symmetric under $z\mapsto\bar z$.

**(a)** Define $g(z)=\overline{f(\bar z)}$ on $D$. Near any $a\in D$, $f(z)=\sum c_n(z-\bar a)^n$ near $\bar a$, so $g(z)=\sum\bar c_n(z-a)^n$; thus $g$ is holomorphic on $D$. For real $x$, $g(x)=\overline{f(x)}=f(x)$ since $f$ is real there. By the identity theorem ($D$ connected, $g=f$ on $\mathbb R$) we get $g=f$, i.e. $f(\bar z)=\overline{f(z)}$.

If $-1<\operatorname{Im}z<0$ then $0<\operatorname{Im}\bar z<1$, so
$$\operatorname{Im}f(z)=\operatorname{Im}\overline{f(\bar z)}=-\operatorname{Im}f(\bar z)<0 .$$

**(b)** Since $f$ is real on $\mathbb R$, $f'(x)=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(x+t)-f(x)}{t}$ ($t$ real) is real. Computing the same complex derivative along the vertical direction,
$$f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{f(x+ih)-f(x)}{ih},\qquad\text{so}\qquad f'(x)=\operatorname{Re}f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0^+}\frac{\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)}{h}\ge0,$$
because $f(x)$ is real and $\operatorname{Im}f(x+ih)>0$ for $0<h<1$.

**(c)** Suppose $f'(c)=0$ for some real $c$. $f-f(c)$ is not identically $0$ (it has positive imaginary part in the upper strip), so near $c$
$$f(z)=f(c)+a_m(z-c)^m\bigl(1+u(z)\bigr),\qquad m\ge2,\ a_m\neq 0,\ u(c)=0,\ u \text{ continuous},$$
and all Taylor coefficients are real because $f^{(n)}(c)$ is a limit of real difference quotients along $\mathbb R$. For $z=c+\varepsilon e^{i\theta}$ with $\theta\in(0,\pi)$,
$$\operatorname{Im}f(z)=a_m\varepsilon^m\operatorname{Im}\!\bigl(e^{im\theta}(1+u(z))\bigr)=a_m\varepsilon^m\bigl(\sin m\theta+O(|u(z)|)\bigr).$$
Since $m\ge2$, $m\theta$ ranges over $(0,m\pi)\supseteq(0,2\pi)$, so we can choose $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ with $a_m\sin m\theta_0=-|a_m|$ ($m\theta_0=\pi/2$ or $3\pi/2$). For $\varepsilon$ small, $|u|<\frac12$ on the circle $|z-c|=\varepsilon$, so $\operatorname{Im}f(c+\varepsilon e^{i\theta_0})\le-\tfrac12|a_m|\varepsilon^m<0$ at a point of the upper strip. This contradicts the hypothesis. Hence $f'(c)\neq 0$, and by (b) $f'(c)>0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt: Prove or disprove: For any $2\times2$ matrix $A$ over $\mathbb C$, there is a $2\times2$ matrix $B$ such that $A=B^2$.
answer: False: $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has no square root, since $B^2=A$ forces $B$ nilpotent, hence $B^2=0\neq A$.

solutions.title: Nilpotency
solutions.body: **The statement is false.** Let $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$, so $A\neq 0$ and $A^2=0$. Suppose $B^2=A$. Then $B^4=A^2=0$, so $B$ is nilpotent, and its only eigenvalue is $0$. Its characteristic polynomial is therefore $x^2$, and by Cayley–Hamilton $B^2=0$. Thus $A=B^2=0$, a contradiction. So no such $B$ exists. $\blacksquare$

solutions.title: Jordan form
solutions.body: If $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $B$ with eigenvector $v$, then $Av=B^2v=\lambda^2v$, so $\lambda^2$ is an eigenvalue of $A$. The only eigenvalue of $A=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ is $0$, hence the only eigenvalue of $B$ is $0$. By Jordan form, $B=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}0&c\\0&0\end{pmatrix}P$ with $c\in\{0,1\}$, and then $B^2=P^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}0&c\\0&0\end{pmatrix}^2P=0\neq  A$. So $A$ has no square root. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, and let $T:V\to V$ be a linear transformation. Assume that:

1. $\langle x,y\rangle=0\implies\langle T(x),T(y)\rangle=0$ for all $x,y\in V$, and
2. there is at least one nonzero $v\in V$ for which $\|T(v)\|=\|v\|$.

Show that $T$ is orthogonal (i.e., $\langle T(x),T(y)\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle$ for all $x,y\in V$).
answer: Extend $u=v/\|v\|$ to an orthonormal basis $x_1=u,x_2,\dots,x_n$. Since $x_1+x_i\perp x_1-x_i$, also $T(x_1)+T(x_i)\perp T(x_1)-T(x_i)$, i.e. $\|T(x_i)\|=\|T(x_1)\|=1$; so $T$ maps an orthonormal basis to an orthonormal basis.

solutions.title: Orthonormal basis through $v$
solutions.body:
Let $u=v/\|v\|$; by linearity $\|T(u)\|=\|u\|=1$. By Gram–Schmidt choose an orthonormal basis $x_1=u,x_2,\dots,x_n$ of $V$. By (1), the vectors $T(x_1),\dots,T(x_n)$ are pairwise orthogonal.

**Claim:** $\|T(x_i)\|=1$ for all $i$. For $i=1$ this is given. For $i>1$, since $x_1\perp x_i$ and $\|x_1\|=\|x_i\|=1$,
$$\langle x_1+x_i,\ x_1-x_i\rangle=\|x_1\|^2-\|x_i\|^2=0 .$$
By (1), $\langle T(x_1)+T(x_i),\,T(x_1)-T(x_i)\rangle=0$. Expanding, and using $T(x_1)\perp T(x_i)$,
$$0=\|T(x_1)\|^2-\|T(x_i)\|^2=1-\|T(x_i)\|^2 ,$$
so $\|T(x_i)\|=1$.

Hence $\langle T(x_i),T(x_j)\rangle=\delta_{ij}=\langle x_i,x_j\rangle$ for all $i,j$. For $x=\sum a_ix_i$, $y=\sum b_jx_j$, bilinearity gives
$$\langle T(x),T(y)\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\langle T(x_i),T(x_j)\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ib_j\langle x_i,x_j\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle .$$
So $T$ is orthogonal. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Let $k$ be a field, let $k[x]$ denote the polynomial ring in one variable over $k$ (as usual), and let $I$ be an ideal in $k[x]$. Show that if $k[x]/I$ is a field, then it is a finite extension of $k$.

In solving this problem, you may only use elementary properties of $k[x]$ (in other words, do not solve this problem by citing a more general theorem that implies this problem as a special case).
answer:
$I
eq 0$ because $k[x]$ is not a field ($x$ has no inverse); for $0
eq  f\in I$, division with remainder shows $k[x]/I$ is spanned over $k$ by $1,x,\dots,x^{\deg f-1}$. Also $k	o k[x]/I$ is injective since $I
eq k[x]$.

solutions.title: Division with remainder
solutions.body:
**$I
eq 0$.** If $I=0$ then $k[x]/I\cong k[x]$, which is not a field: $x$ has no inverse, since $\deg(xg)=1+\deg g\ge1$ for every nonzero $g$, so $xg
eq 1$.

**$k$ embeds.** A field has $1
eq 0$, so $1
otin I$. The composite $k	o k[x]	o k[x]/I$ is a ring homomorphism from a field; its kernel is an ideal of $k$ not containing $1$, hence $0$. So $k[x]/I$ is an extension field of $k$.

**Finite dimension.** Pick $0
eq  f\in I$ of degree $d$ (note $d\ge1$, since a nonzero constant in $I$ would give $1\in I$). For any $g\in k[x]$, division with remainder gives $g=qf+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<d$. Then $g\equiv r\pmod I$, so every class in $k[x]/I$ is a $k$-linear combination of the classes of $1,x,\dots,x^{d-1}$. Hence $[k[x]/I:k]\le d<\infty$, i.e. $k[x]/I$ is a finite extension of $k$. $ lacksquare$

prompt:
Let $G$ be a group whose order is twice an odd number. For $g\in G$, let $\lambda_g$ denote the permutation of $G$ given by $\lambda_g(x)=gx$ for $x\in G$.

(a) Let $g$ be in $G$. Prove that the permutation $\lambda_g$ is even if and only if the order of $g$ is odd.

(b) Let $N=\{g\in G:\operatorname{order}(g)\text{ is odd}\}$. Prove that $N$ is a normal subgroup of $G$ of index 2.
answer: (a) $\lambda_g$ is a product of $2n/m$ disjoint $m$-cycles ($|G|=2n$, $n$ odd, $m=\operatorname{ord}g$), so its sign is $(-1)^{(m-1)2n/m}$, which is $-1$ iff $m$ is even. (b) $N$ is the kernel of $g\mapsto\operatorname{sgn}(\lambda_g)$, which is onto $\{\pm1\}$ by Cauchy's theorem.

solutions.title: Cycle structure of the regular representation
solutions.body:
Write $|G|=2n$ with $n$ odd.

**(a)** Let $m$ be the order of $g$. The orbits of $\langle\lambda_g\rangle$ on $G$ are the right cosets $\langle g\rangle x=\{x,gx,\dots,g^{m-1}x\}$, each of size exactly $m$ (since $g^ix=g^jx\iff g^i=g^j$). So $\lambda_g$ is a product of $2n/m$ disjoint $m$-cycles. An $m$-cycle has sign $(-1)^{m-1}$, so
$$\operatorname{sgn}\lambda_g=(-1)^{(m-1)\cdot 2n/m}.$$
If $m$ is odd, $m-1$ is even and $\lambda_g$ is even. If $m$ is even, then $m-1$ is odd, and $2n/m$ is odd because $m\mid 2n$ with $m$ even means $m=2m'$ with $m'\mid n$, so $2n/m=n/m'$ is odd; thus $\lambda_g$ is odd.

**(b)** The map $g\mapsto\lambda_g$ is a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(G)$, since $\lambda_{gh}=\lambda_g\lambda_h$. Composing with the sign homomorphism gives a homomorphism
$$\varepsilon:G\to\{\pm1\},\qquad \varepsilon(g)=\operatorname{sgn}\lambda_g .$$
By (a), $\ker\varepsilon=\{g:\operatorname{ord}g\text{ odd}\}=N$. As a kernel, $N$ is a normal subgroup. Since $2\mid|G|$, Cauchy's theorem gives an element $g$ of order $2$; by (a) $\varepsilon(g)=-1$, so $\varepsilon$ is surjective and $[G:N]=|\{\pm1\}|=2$. $\blacksquare$

answer: If $f(x_1)>1$, let $a=\sup\{x<x_1:f(x)\le1\}$; then $f(a)=1$ and $f>1$ on $(a,x_1]$, and the mean value theorem on $[a,x_1]$ gives $f(x_1)-1=f'(\xi)(x_1-a)\le0$, a contradiction.

solutions.title: Last time $f$ was at most 1
solutions.body:
Suppose, for contradiction, that $f(x_1)>1$ for some $x_1\ge0$; then $x_1>0$ since $f(0)=1$. The set $\{x\in[0,x_1]:f(x)\le1\}$ contains $0$ and is closed (by continuity), so it has a largest element $a<x_1$. Then $f(a)\le1$, and $f(x)>1$ for all $x\in(a,x_1]$; by continuity $f(a)\ge1$, so $f(a)=1$.

By the mean value theorem on $[a,x_1]$ (continuity on $[a,x_1]$, differentiability on $(a,x_1)\subseteq(0,\infty)$) there is $\xi\in(a,x_1)$ with
$$f(x_1)-1=f(x_1)-f(a)=f'(\xi)(x_1-a).$$
Since $f(\xi)>1$ and $\xi>0$, the hypothesis gives $f'(\xi)\le0$, so $f(x_1)\le1$, a contradiction. Hence $f(x)\le1$ for all $x\ge0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Let $f:\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ be defined by
$$f(x,y)=\begin{cases}x^{4/3}\sin(y/x)&\text{if }x\neq 0,\\ 0&\text{if }x=0.\end{cases}$$
Determine all points at which $f$ is differentiable.
answer: $f$ is differentiable at every point of $\mathbb R^2$: away from $x=0$ it is a composition of smooth functions, and at $(0,y_0)$ we have $|f(h_1,y_0+h_2)|\le|h_1|^{4/3}=o(\|h\|)$, so $Df(0,y_0)=0$.

solutions.title: Smooth part and a direct estimate on the axis
solutions.body:
**Points with $x\neq 0$.** On the open set $\{x\neq 0\}$, $f$ is built from differentiable functions ($x\mapsto x^{4/3}=(x^{1/3})^4$ is differentiable for $x\neq 0$, and $(x,y)\mapsto\sin(y/x)$ is smooth there), so $f$ is differentiable at every such point.

**Points $(0,y_0)$.** For all $(x,y)$ we have $|f(x,y)|\le|x|^{4/3}$ (trivially if $x=0$). For $h=(h_1,h_2)\neq 0$,
$$\frac{|f(0+h_1,y_0+h_2)-f(0,y_0)-0|}{\|h\|}=\frac{|f(h_1,y_0+h_2)|}{\|h\|}\le\frac{|h_1|^{4/3}}{\|h\|}\le|h_1|^{1/3}\le\|h\|^{1/3}\xrightarrow[h\to0]{}0$$
(when $h_1=0$ the quotient is $0$). Therefore $f$ is differentiable at $(0,y_0)$ with derivative the zero linear map.

**Answer:** $f$ is differentiable at **every point of $\mathbb R^2$**. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ which is analytic in a neighborhood of $0$. Let its Maclaurin series be
$$\sum_{k=0}^\infty a_kz^k$$
with all $a_k\ge0$. Suppose there is a pole of modulus $r>0$ and that no pole has modulus $<r$. Prove that there is a pole at $z=r$.
answer: (Pringsheim.) The series converges for $|z|<r$. If $rw$ ($|w|=1$) is a pole then $|f((1-\varepsilon)rw)|\to\infty$, but $|f((1-\varepsilon)rw)|\le\sum a_k((1-\varepsilon)r)^k=f((1-\varepsilon)r)$, so $f$ is unbounded near $r$, so $r$ is a pole.

solutions.title: Compare with the positive real axis
solutions.body:
Since $f$ has no poles in $|z|<r$, it is holomorphic on the disc $|z|<r$, so its Maclaurin series converges to $f$ there.

Let $rw$, $|w|=1$, be a pole of modulus $r$. Then $|f(z)|\to\infty$ as $z\to rw$, in particular $|f((1-\varepsilon)rw)|\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$. For $0<\varepsilon<1$, using $a_k\ge0$,
$$|f((1-\varepsilon)rw)|=\Bigl|\sum_k a_k(1-\varepsilon)^kr^kw^k\Bigr|\le\sum_k a_k(1-\varepsilon)^kr^k=f((1-\varepsilon)r).$$
Hence $f((1-\varepsilon)r)\to\infty$ as $\varepsilon\to0^+$, so $f$ is not bounded near $z=r$ and cannot be analytic at $r$. Since $f$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$, its only non-analytic points are poles, so $z=r$ is a pole. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Compute
$$\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_C\frac{dz}{\sin\frac1z},$$
where $C$ is the circle $|z|=\frac15$, positively oriented.

solutions.title: Substitute $w=1/z$
solutions.body:
The integrand has poles at $z=\frac1{k\pi}$ accumulating at $0$, which is not an isolated singularity, so we move to $w=1/z$. On $C$ there are no zeros of $\sin(1/z)$ since $5\neq k\pi$.

With $z=1/w$, $dz=-dw/w^2$, and the positively oriented circle $|z|=\frac15$ becomes the circle $|w|=5$ traversed **negatively**. The two sign changes cancel:
$$\frac1{2\pi i}\int_C\frac{dz}{\sin(1/z)}=\frac1{2\pi i}\oint_{|w|=5}\frac{dw}{w^2\sin w}.$$
Inside $|w|<5$ the zeros of $w^2\sin w$ are $w=0$ and $w=\pm\pi$ (since $2\pi>5$).

- At $w=\pm\pi$ (simple poles): residue $\dfrac{1}{(w^2\sin w)'}\Big|_{\pm\pi}=\dfrac{1}{2w\sin w+w^2\cos w}\Big|_{\pm\pi}=\dfrac1{\pi^2\cos(\pm\pi)}=-\dfrac1{\pi^2}$.
- At $w=0$ (triple pole): $\dfrac{1}{w^2\sin w}=\dfrac{1}{w^3}\Bigl(1-\dfrac{w^2}{6}+\dots\Bigr)^{-1}=\dfrac1{w^3}+\dfrac{1}{6w}+\dots$, residue $\frac16$.

By the residue theorem,
$$\frac1{2\pi i}\int_C\frac{dz}{\sin(1/z)}=\frac16-\frac{2}{\pi^2}\approx-0.03598 .$$
(A numerical evaluation of the contour integral agrees.)

**Answer:** $\dfrac16-\dfrac2{\pi^2}$.

solutions.title: Residues outside $C$ and at infinity
solutions.body:
Inside $|z|<\frac15$ the integrand $1/\sin(1/z)$ has infinitely many poles $z_k=\frac1{k\pi}$, $|k|\ge2$, accumulating at $0$; outside $C$ it has only the poles $\pm\frac1\pi$ (since $\frac1{2\pi}<\frac15<\frac1\pi$). So use the exterior form of the residue theorem: $\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_C=-\bigl(\sum_{|z|>1/5}\operatorname{Res}+\operatorname{Res}_{\infty}\bigr)$.

- At $z_{\pm1}=\pm\frac1\pi$: $\frac{d}{dz}\sin(1/z)=-\frac{\cos(1/z)}{z^2}$, so the residue is $\dfrac{1}{-\pi^2\cos(\pm\pi)}=\dfrac1{\pi^2}$ each.
- At $\infty$: for large $z$, $\dfrac1{\sin(1/z)}=z\Bigl(1-\dfrac1{6z^2}+\dots\Bigr)^{-1}=z+\dfrac{1}{6z}+\dots$, so $\operatorname{Res}_\infty=-\frac16$.

Hence the integral equals $-\bigl(\frac2{\pi^2}-\frac16\bigr)=\frac16-\frac2{\pi^2}$, as before.

**Answer:** $\dfrac16-\dfrac2{\pi^2}$.

prompt: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $F$, and let $L:V\to V$ be a linear transformation. Suppose that the characteristic polynomial $\chi$ of $L$ is written as $\chi=\chi_1\chi_2$ where $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ are two relatively prime polynomials with coefficients in $F$. Show that $V$ can be written as the direct sum of two subspaces $V_1$ and $V_2$ with the property that $\chi_i(L)V_i=0$ for $i=1,2$.
answer: $V_i=\ker\chi_i(L)$. Write $p_1\chi_1+p_2\chi_2=1$; then $v=p_2(L)\chi_2(L)v+p_1(L)\chi_1(L)v$ splits $v$ into parts in $V_1$ and $V_2$ (by Cayley–Hamilton), and $V_1\cap V_2=0$.

solutions.title: Bézout identity and Cayley–Hamilton
solutions.body:
Let $V_i=\ker\chi_i(L)$ for $i=1,2$; then $\chi_i(L)V_i=0$ by definition. Since $\gcd(\chi_1,\chi_2)=1$ in the PID $F[t]$, there are $p_1,p_2\in F[t]$ with
$$p_1\chi_1+p_2\chi_2=1,\qquad\text{so}\qquad p_1(L)\chi_1(L)+p_2(L)\chi_2(L)=I .$$
Recall that polynomials in $L$ commute with each other.

**$V_1\cap V_2=0$.** If $v\in V_1\cap V_2$ then $v=p_1(L)\chi_1(L)v+p_2(L)\chi_2(L)v=0+0=0$.

**$V_1+V_2=V$.** Given $v\in V$, put $v_1=p_2(L)\chi_2(L)v$ and $v_2=p_1(L)\chi_1(L)v$. Then $v_1+v_2=v$, and by the Cayley–Hamilton theorem $\chi(L)=0$, so
$$\chi_1(L)v_1=p_2(L)\chi_1(L)\chi_2(L)v=p_2(L)\chi(L)v=0,$$
i.e. $v_1\in V_1$; similarly $v_2\in V_2$.

Therefore $V=V_1\oplus V_2$ with $\chi_i(L)V_i=0$. $\blacksquare$

prompt:
Show that an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ of complex numbers satisfying
$$|a_{ii}|>\sum_{j\neq  i}|a_{ij}|$$
for all $1\le i\le n$ must be invertible.
answer:
If $Ax=0$ with $x
eq 0$, pick $i$ with $|x_i|$ maximal; the $i$th equation gives $|a_{ii}||x_i|\le\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}||x_j|\le|x_i|\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}|$, contradicting strict diagonal dominance.

solutions.title: Look at the largest coordinate of a kernel vector
solutions.body:
Suppose $A$ is singular, and let $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)^T
eq 0$ with $Ax=0$. Choose $i$ with $|x_i|=\max_j|x_j|>0$. The $i$th coordinate of $Ax=0$ gives $a_{ii}x_i=-\sum_{j
eq  i}a_{ij}x_j$, hence
$$|a_{ii}|\,|x_i|\le\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le|x_i|\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}| .$$
Dividing by $|x_i|>0$ gives $|a_{ii}|\le\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}|$, contradicting the hypothesis. So $A$ is invertible. $ lacksquare$

(Equivalently: by the Gershgorin circle theorem every eigenvalue lies in some disc $|z-a_{ii}|\le\sum_{j
eq  i}|a_{ij}|<|a_{ii}|$, none of which contains $0$.)

prompt: How many roots does the polynomial $x^{100000}-1$ have in the finite field $\mathbb F_{65537}$? ($65537=2^{16}+1$ is a prime.)

solutions.title: Cyclic group of order $2^{16}$
solutions.body:
The roots are the elements $x\in\mathbb F_{65537}^\times$ with $x^{100000}=1$. The group $\mathbb F_{65537}^\times$ is cyclic of order $65536=2^{16}$. In a cyclic group of order $N$, the number of solutions of $x^m=1$ is $\gcd(m,N)$. Here
$$100000=2^5\cdot5^5,\qquad\gcd(2^5\cdot5^5,\ 2^{16})=2^5=32 .$$
So there are $32$ roots. (They are simple: the derivative $100000x^{99999}$ vanishes only at $0$, which is not a root.)

**Answer:** $32$.

solutions.title: Orders of elements
solutions.body:
Every element of $\mathbb F_{65537}^\times$ has order a power of $2$ dividing $2^{16}$. Such an order divides $100000=2^5\cdot5^5$ exactly when it divides $2^5$. So the roots are exactly the solutions of $x^{32}=1$, and in a cyclic group of order $2^{16}$ there are exactly $32$ of them (the subgroup of order $32$). A direct computer count over all of $\mathbb F_{65537}$ also gives $32$.

**Answer:** $32$.

prompt: Let $G$ be a group generated by two elements $a$ and $b$, both of order 2. Prove that $G$ has a subgroup of index 2. (Hint: Show that the set of elements that can be written as the product of an even number of generators is not the whole of G.)
answer: Let $H$ be the set of products of an even number of letters $a,b$; it is a subgroup with $G=H\cup aH$, so $[G:H]\le2$. An odd-length word reduces to an alternating word of odd length, which is a palindrome $u\,x\,u^{-1}$ with $x\in\{a,b\}$, hence $\neq 1$; so $a\notin H$ and $[G:H]=2$.

solutions.title: Odd words are conjugates of generators
solutions.body:
Since $a^{-1}=a$ and $b^{-1}=b$, every element of $G$ is a finite product (word) of the letters $a,b$. Let $H$ be the set of elements expressible as a word of **even** length.

**$H$ is a subgroup of index at most 2.** $1$ is the empty word; concatenating two even words gives an even word; and the inverse of $x_1x_2\cdots x_{2k}$ is $x_{2k}\cdots x_1$ (each letter is its own inverse), again even. Every word is either even or $a$ times an even word, so $G=H\cup aH$ and $[G:H]\le2$. (So $H$ is normal, though we don't need this.)

**$a\notin H$.** If $a\in H$, then $a=w$ for an even word $w$, so $aw^{-1}=1$ with $aw^{-1}$ a word of odd length. We show no odd-length word equals $1$.

Take an odd-length word and repeatedly delete adjacent pairs $aa$ or $bb$ (each equals $1$); this preserves the group element and the parity of the length, so we reach an odd-length word with no two equal adjacent letters, i.e. an **alternating** word $w=x_1x_2\cdots x_{2k+1}$ (it is non-empty, since its length is odd). An alternating word of odd length begins and ends with the same letter and reads the same backwards, so with $u=x_1\cdots x_k$,
$$w=u\,x_{k+1}\,(x_k\cdots x_1)=u\,x_{k+1}\,u^{-1}.$$
This is a conjugate of $x_{k+1}\in\{a,b\}$, which has order $2$, so $w\neq 1$.

Hence $a\notin H$, so $H\neq  G$ and $[G:H]=2$. $\blacksquare$
